title: Chapter 8. Of the Virtues Commonly Called Intellectual; and Their Contrary Defects
paragraphs: Virtue, generally, in any kind of subject, is something valued for its eminence, and it consists in comparison. For if all things existed equally in all men, nothing would be prized. By the intellectual virtues are always meant such abilities of the mind as men praise, value, and wish to have in themselves; they go commonly under the name of a good wit — though the same word 'wit' is also used to mark out one particular ability from the rest.

These virtues are of two sorts: natural, and acquired. By 'natural' I do not mean what a man has from his birth — that is nothing but sense, in which men differ so little from one another, and from brute beasts, that it is not to be counted among the virtues. I mean the wit that is gained by use alone and by experience, without method, cultivation, or instruction. This NATURAL WIT consists principally in two things: speed of imagining (that is, the swift succession of one thought to another) and steady direction toward some approved end. The opposite of these — a slow imagination — produces the defect or fault of the mind that is commonly called DULLNESS, stupidity, and sometimes other names that signify slowness of motion, or difficulty of being moved.

This difference of quickness is caused by the difference of men's passions: they love and dislike, some one thing, some another. So some men's thoughts run one way, some another; they are held by, and they notice differently, the things that pass through their imagination. In this succession of men's thoughts, the only things to notice about what they think on are: in what these things are like one another, in what they are unlike, what they serve for, or how they serve some particular purpose. Those who notice the resemblances, in cases where those resemblances are rarely noticed by others, are said to have a good wit — by which on this occasion is meant a good fancy. But those who notice the differences and unlikenesses — which is called distinguishing, discerning, and judging between thing and thing — in cases where such discernment is not easy, are said to have a good judgement; and particularly in matters of conversation and business, where times, places, and persons must be discerned, this virtue is called DISCRETION. The first, fancy, without the help of judgement, is not praised as a virtue; but the second, judgement and discretion, is praised on its own, without the help of fancy. Beyond the discretion of times, places, and persons necessary for a good fancy, what is also required is a frequent application of one's thoughts to their end — that is, to some use to be made of them. With that done, a man with this virtue will easily be supplied with similitudes that please not only by illustrating his discourse and adorning it with new and apt metaphors, but also by the rarity of their invention. But without steadiness, and direction toward some end, a great fancy is a kind of madness: such as is found in those who, on entering any discourse, are snatched from their purpose by every passing thought, into so many and so long digressions and parentheses that they utterly lose themselves. For this kind of folly I know no particular name; but its causes are sometimes a lack of experience (which makes things seem new and rare to the man which do not seem so to others), and sometimes pusillanimity (which makes things seem great to him which other men think trifling). And whatever is new or great, and so seems worth telling, draws a man by degrees away from the intended course of his discourse.

In a good poem, whether epic or dramatic, and likewise in sonnets, epigrams, and other pieces, both judgement and fancy are required; but the fancy must be the more conspicuous, because such works please by extravagance, but ought not to displease by indiscretion.

In a good history, the judgement must be conspicuous, because what makes a history good lies in the method, in the truth, and in the choice of those actions most worth knowing. Fancy has no place except in the adornment of style.

In orations of praise, and in invectives, the fancy is dominant, because the design is not truth but to honour or dishonour, and this is done by noble or by vile comparisons. The judgement only suggests which circumstances make an action laudable or culpable.
In exhortations and pleadings, as truth or disguise serves best the design in hand, so judgement or fancy is most required.

In demonstration, in counsel, and in any rigorous search for truth, judgement does everything — except that sometimes the understanding needs to be opened by an apt comparison, and there fancy has some use. But metaphors in such cases are excluded altogether: since they openly profess to deceive, to admit them into counsel or reasoning is plain folly.

And in any discourse whatever, if the lack of discretion is plain, then however extravagant the fancy may be, the whole discourse will be taken as a sign of want of wit; and it will never be so taken when the discretion is plain, no matter how ordinary the fancy.

The secret thoughts of a man run over all things, holy, profane, clean, obscene, grave, and light, without shame or blame — which verbal discourse cannot do, beyond what judgement shall approve as to time, place, and persons. An anatomist or a physician may speak, or write, his judgement on unclean things, because the aim is not to please but to profit. But for another man to write his extravagant and amusing fancies on the same matters is as if a man, after being tumbled into the dirt, should come and present himself before good company. The difference is only one of discretion. Again, in deliberately relaxed mind and in familiar company, a man may play with the sounds and the equivocal meanings of words — sometimes with strikes of extraordinary fancy. But in a sermon, in public, or before persons unknown or whom we ought to revere, no jingling of words will not be accounted folly: and again the difference is only the lack of discretion. So where wit is wanting, it is not fancy that is wanting but discretion. Judgement therefore without fancy is wit, but fancy without judgement is not.

When the thoughts of a man with a project in hand, running over a multitude of things, observe how those things contribute to that project, or to what other project they might contribute, then if his observations are such as are not easy or usual, this wit of his is called PRUDENCE. It depends on much experience and on the memory of similar things and their previous consequences. In this there is not so much difference between men as there is in their fancy and their judgement, because the experience of men equal in age is not very unequal in quantity, but lies in different occasions; each man has his own private designs. To govern well a household, or a kingdom, are not different degrees of prudence but different sorts of business — no more than to draw a picture in miniature, or as great as, or greater than, life are different degrees of art. A plain farmer is more prudent in the affairs of his own house than a privy councillor is in the affairs of another man.

If to prudence you add the use of unjust or dishonest means — such as are usually prompted by fear or want — you have that crooked wisdom which is called CRAFT, and which is a sign of pusillanimity. For magnanimity is contempt of unjust or dishonest helps. And what the Latins call versutia (translated into English as 'shifting'), which is the putting off of a present danger or inconvenience by entering on a greater — as when a man robs Peter to pay Paul — is only a shorter-sighted craft. The name versutia comes from versura, which means borrowing money at interest for the present payment of interest.

As for acquired wit — by which I mean wit acquired by method and instruction — there is none but reason, which is grounded on the right use of speech and which produces the sciences. But of reason and science I have already spoken in the fifth and sixth chapters.

The causes of this difference of wits lie in the passions; and the difference of passions arises partly from the different constitution of the body, and partly from different education. For if the difference came from the temper of the brain and the organs of sense, inner or outer, there would be no less difference between men in their sight, hearing, or other senses than there is in their fancies and discretions. It comes therefore from the passions, which differ not only because of the difference of men's constitutions but also from differences of customs and education.

The passions that most of all cause the differences of wit are principally the greater or lesser desire of power, of riches, of knowledge, and of honour. All of these can be reduced to the first — the desire of power. For riches, knowledge, and honour are only different sorts of power.

Therefore a man who has no great passion for any of these things, but is (as men call it) indifferent — though he may be so far a good man as to be free from giving offence — cannot possibly have either a great fancy or much judgement. For the thoughts are to the desires as scouts and spies sent abroad to find the way to the things desired: all steadiness in the motion of the mind, and all quickness in it, come from there. To have no desire is to be dead; to have weak passions is dullness; to have passions indifferently for everything is GIDDINESS and distraction; and to have stronger and more violent passions for some thing than are ordinarily seen in others is what men call MADNESS.

Of madness there are almost as many kinds as there are passions. Sometimes the extraordinary and extravagant passion comes from the bad constitution of the bodily organs, or from harm done to them; and sometimes the harm and disorder of the organs is caused by the violence or long continuance of the passion. But in both cases the madness is of one and the same nature.
The passion whose violence or continuance produces madness is either great vainglory (commonly called pride and self-conceit) or great dejection of mind.

Pride exposes a man to anger, the excess of which is the madness called RAGE, or FURY. And so it comes about that excessive desire of revenge, when it becomes habitual, damages the organs and becomes rage; that excessive love, joined with jealousy, also becomes rage; that an excessive opinion of one's own self — for divine inspiration, for wisdom, learning, beauty, and the like — becomes distraction and giddiness; the same, joined with envy, becomes rage; and a violent opinion of the truth of anything that is contradicted by others becomes rage.

Dejection exposes a man to groundless fears, which is a madness commonly called MELANCHOLY, also showing itself in various ways: in haunting solitudes and graves, in superstitious behaviour, in fearing some one or another particular thing. In short, all passions that produce strange and unusual behaviour are called by the general name of madness. As for the various kinds of madness, anyone willing to take the trouble might enrol a legion. And if the excesses are madness, there is no doubt that the passions themselves, when they tend to evil, are degrees of the same.

For example: though the effect of folly in those who hold the opinion that they are inspired is not always visible in any one man through some very extravagant action springing from such a passion, yet when many of them conspire together, the rage of the whole multitude is visible enough. For what greater sign of madness can there be than to clamour, strike, and throw stones at our best friends? Yet this is something less than what such a multitude will do; for they will clamour, fight against, and destroy those by whom, all their lives before, they have been protected and kept safe from injury. And if this is madness in the multitude, it is the same in every individual man. For as in the middle of the sea, though a man perceives no sound from the part of the water right next to him, yet he is well assured that this part contributes as much to the roaring of the sea as any other part of the same volume — so also, though we perceive no great unquietness in one or two men, we may be well assured that their individual passions are parts of the seditious roaring of a troubled nation. And if there were nothing else to betray their madness, the very fact that they claim such inspiration for themselves is argument enough. If some man in Bedlam should entertain you with sober talk, and on taking leave you should want to know who he was, so that another time you could repay his civility, and he should tell you he was God the Father — I think you would need to expect no extravagant action as further proof of his madness.

This opinion of inspiration, commonly called Private Spirit, often begins from some lucky hitting on an error generally held by others. Not knowing — or not remembering — what process of reasoning led them to so singular a truth (as they take it to be, though often it is an untruth they have lighted on), they immediately admire themselves as being in the special grace of God Almighty, who has supernaturally revealed it to them by his Spirit.

Again, that madness is nothing but too much visible passion can be inferred from the effects of wine, which are the same as those of the bad disposition of the organs. The variety of behaviour in men who have drunk too much is the same as that of madmen: some raging, some loving, some laughing, all extravagantly, but according to their several dominant passions. The effect of wine is only to remove dissimulation, and to take from them the sight of the deformity of their passions. For (I believe) the most sober men, when they walk alone without care and without occupation of the mind, would be unwilling to have the vanity and extravagance of their thoughts at such a time made public — which is a confession that passions unguided are for the most part sheer madness.

The opinions of the world, in ancient and in later ages, about the cause of madness, have been two. Some derive it from the passions; some from daemons, or spirits, either good or bad, which they thought might enter into a man, possess him, and move his organs in the strange and uncouth ways madmen do. The first sort, therefore, called such men madmen; but the second called them sometimes daemoniacks (that is, possessed with spirits), sometimes energumeni (that is, agitated or moved by spirits); and in Italy today they are called not only pazzi, madmen, but also spiritati, men possessed.

There was once a great gathering of people in Abdera, a city of the Greeks, at the performance of the tragedy of Andromeda, on an extremely hot day. As a result, a great many of the spectators, falling into fevers, suffered this peculiar consequence from the heat and the tragedy together: they did nothing but recite iambic verses, with the names of Perseus and Andromeda. This, along with the fever, was cured by the coming on of winter. And the madness was thought to come from the passion imprinted by the tragedy. Likewise a fit of madness once raged in another Greek city, seizing only the young maidens, and causing many of them to hang themselves. Most at the time thought this an act of the devil. But one man, suspecting that this contempt of life might come from some passion of the mind, and supposing that they did not also despise their honour, advised the magistrates to strip the bodies of those who had so hanged themselves and let them hang out naked. This, the story says, cured the madness. But on the other side, those same Greeks often ascribed madness to the operation of the Eumenides, or Furies — and sometimes of Ceres, Phoebus, and other gods. So far did men attribute reality to phantasms, taking them to be airy living bodies, and generally calling them spirits. And as the Romans on this point held the same opinion as the Greeks, so also did the Jews; for they called madmen prophets, or (depending on whether they thought the spirits good or bad) daemoniacks. Some of them called both prophets and daemoniacks madmen; and some called the same man both daemoniack and madman. As for the Gentiles, it is no wonder; for diseases and health, vices and virtues, and many natural accidents, were among them named and worshipped as daemons. So that by 'daemon' a man might understand, on occasion, an ague as well as a devil. But for the Jews to have such an opinion is somewhat strange. For neither Moses nor Abraham claimed to prophesy by the possession of a spirit, but from the voice of God, or by a vision or dream; nor is there anything in his Law, moral or ceremonial, by which they were taught that there is any such enthusiasm, or any possession. When God is said (Numbers 11:25) to take from the spirit that was in Moses, and to give it to the seventy elders, the Spirit of God (taking it for the substance of God) is not divided. By 'the Spirit of God' in a man, the Scriptures mean a man's spirit inclined to godliness. And where it is said (Exodus 28:3) 'whom I have filled with the spirit of wisdom to make garments for Aaron,' what is meant is not a spirit put into them that can make garments, but the wisdom of their own spirits in that kind of work. In the same sense, the spirit of a man, when it produces unclean actions, is ordinarily called an unclean spirit; and so other spirits, though not always, yet as often as the virtue or vice so named is extraordinary and eminent. Nor did the other prophets of the Old Testament claim enthusiasm, or that God spoke in them; they claimed that he spoke to them by voice, vision, or dream; and the burden of the Lord was not possession but command. How then could the Jews fall into this opinion of possession? I can imagine no reason but the one common to all men: lack of curiosity to search for natural causes, and the placing of felicity in the acquisition of the coarse pleasures of the senses, and of the things that most directly conduce to those pleasures. For those who see any strange and unusual ability or defect in a man's mind, unless they also see from what cause it might probably proceed, can hardly think it natural; and if not natural, they must think it supernatural; and then what can it be but that either God or the devil is in him? Hence it came about that, when our Saviour (Mark 3:21) was surrounded by the multitude, those of his household feared he was mad and went out to restrain him; but the scribes said he had Beelzebub, and that this was how he cast out devils — as if the greater madman had cowed the lesser. And again (John 10:20) some said, 'He has a devil, and is mad,' whereas others, holding him for a prophet, said, 'These are not the words of one that has a devil.' So too in the Old Testament: he who came to anoint Jehu (2 Kings 9:11) was a prophet, but some of the company asked Jehu, 'What did that madman come for?' In short, it is plain that whoever behaved in an extraordinary way was thought by the Jews to be possessed either with a good or with an evil spirit — except by the Sadducees, who erred so far on the other side as not to believe there were any spirits at all (which is very close to outright atheism), and so perhaps the more provoked others to call such men daemoniacks rather than madmen.

But why then does our Saviour proceed to cure them as though they were possessed, and not as though they were mad? To this I can give no other kind of answer than the one given to those who press Scripture against the opinion that the earth moves. Scripture was written to show men the kingdom of God and to prepare their minds to become his obedient subjects, leaving the world and the philosophy of it to the disputation of men, for the exercise of their natural reason. Whether it is the motion of the earth or of the sun that makes day and night, or whether the disorderly actions of men come from passion or from the devil (so long as we do not worship him), it makes no difference to our obedience and subjection to God Almighty — which is the thing for which Scripture was written. As for our Saviour speaking to the disease as if to a person, that is the usual phrase of all who cure by words only, as Christ did (and as enchanters pretend to do, whether or not they really speak to a devil). For is not Christ also said (Matthew 8:26) to have rebuked the winds? Is he not also said (Luke 4:39) to rebuke a fever? Yet this does not argue that a fever is a devil. And whereas many of these devils are said to have confessed Christ, there is no need to interpret those passages as anything more than that those madmen confessed him. And whereas our Saviour (Matthew 12:43) speaks of an unclean spirit which, having gone out of a man, wanders through dry places, seeking rest and finding none, and returns into the same man with seven other spirits worse than itself — this is plainly a parable, alluding to a man who, after some little effort to give up his lusts, is overcome by their strength and becomes seven times worse than he was. So I see nothing at all in Scripture that requires us to believe that daemoniacks were anything other than madmen.

There is yet another fault in the discourses of some men, which may also be counted among the sorts of madness — namely, the abuse of words, of which I spoke before in the fifth chapter under the name of absurdity. This happens when men speak words which, put together, have no signification at all, but which have been hit upon either by some, through misunderstanding the words they have received and repeat by rote, or by others, from a deliberate intention to deceive by obscurity. This falls only to those who deal in questions of incomprehensible matters, like the Schoolmen, or in questions of abstruse philosophy. The common sort of men seldom speak insignificantly, and are therefore by those other distinguished persons counted idiots. But to be assured that the Schoolmen's words have nothing in the mind to correspond to them, some examples are needed. If anyone wants them, let him take a Schoolman in hand and see if he can translate any chapter on any difficult point — the Trinity, the Deity, the nature of Christ, transubstantiation, free will, and so on — into any modern tongue so as to make it intelligible; or into any tolerable Latin, such as those were familiar with who lived when Latin was the common tongue. What does it mean to say, 'The first cause does not necessarily inflow anything into the second, by virtue of the essential subordination of the second causes, by which it may help it to work'? That is the translation of the title of the sixth chapter of Suárez's first book, Of the Concourse, Motion, and Help of God. When men write whole volumes of such stuff, are they not mad, or do they not intend to make others so? In particular, in the question of transubstantiation: when, after certain words spoken, those who say that the whiteness, roundness, magnitude, quality, corruptibility — all of which are incorporeal — leave the wafer and enter the body of our blessed Saviour, do they not make those 'nesses' and 'tudes' and 'ties' into so many spirits possessing his body? For by spirits they always mean things that, being incorporeal, are nevertheless able to move from one place to another. So this kind of absurdity may rightly be counted among the many sorts of madness; and all the time when, guided by clear thoughts of their worldly lust, they refrain from disputing or writing in this way, those are only lucid intervals. And so much for the intellectual virtues and defects.
